title: The Case for AI LTS: Why the Real World Needs a Stable Release Cycle
content:
OCT 2026 — BEVERLEY · THINKING
The Case for AI LTS: Why the Real World Needs a Stable Release Cycle
On what a college loses when a model is deprecated, and the case for a supported release that stays where it is.
If you spend enough time around the current discourse in artificial intelligence, it is easy to get the impression that the only metric that matters is the frontier. Every few weeks, the industry holds its breath for a new leaderboard topper. A model arrives with a larger context window, a few percentage points gained on a coding benchmark, or a faster time-to-first-token, and the ecosystem is expected to reconsider its tools, rewrite its prompts and migrate.
In my response to Dario Amodei's We Must Pace the Frontier, I argued that slowing the pace of frontier development serves a purpose beyond giving researchers more time to make AI safe. It gives the rest of us time to absorb what already exists: to learn how these systems behave, build practices around them, and make them part of working lives and institutions.
Even when we have a capable system, why should we have to keep replacing it?
The AI industry needs the equivalent of an Ubuntu Long Term Support (LTS) release: a stable, maintained version that organisations can depend on for years, while development continues at the frontier.
Two release cycles, two different purposes
Linux settled this a long time ago. Run a rolling release and you get the newest kernel, the newest packages and the occasional breakage, which is part of the bargain. Run infrastructure that other people depend on and novelty stops being an advantage: what you want is a defined support period, predictable maintenance, and changes that do not casually break existing work. Ubuntu designates a long-term support release every two years and maintains it for five, which has never stopped Canonical shipping interim releases for anyone who wants them.
A supported release is not a frozen one. Vulnerabilities get fixed, bugs get addressed, supported components get updates. The commitment is to maintain a known release rather than continually replace it with the newest one.
AI has no comparable commitment. Pinned model snapshots and enterprise deprecation windows provide some stability, but pinning a version is not a guarantee of long-term availability, maintenance and compatibility.
The nearest thing anyone has offered is Anthropic's undertaking, published in November 2025, to preserve the weights of all publicly released models for at least the lifetime of the company. That matters, and it answers a different question. Preserved weights protect the model. A support window protects the people who built their work around it.
The cost of moving ground
Consider how a school, further education college or NHS trust actually operates. These organisations are not resistant to change because the people inside them lack imagination. They are cautious because the cost of failure is high, budgets are constrained, and the consequences of disruption fall on people who may have little power to absorb it.
Imagine a college spending six months developing an accessible teaching workflow around a particular model. Staff are trained. Safeguarding procedures are written. The model is tested against complex student queries. Guidance is developed for students with additional needs, and teachers learn which instructions work, where the model makes mistakes and when its answers need checking. Every one of those decisions turns on the question I put in The Scribe Rule, whether a given use removes a barrier or removes the lesson, and it has to be answered for the model actually in front of you.
The workflow begins to work. Staff become familiar with it, and students develop routines that allow them to work more independently.
Then the model is deprecated, its behaviour changes materially, or its replacement handles familiar tasks differently. The college must reassess its procedures, retrain staff and test the new system. Some of the work has to be done again, and the disruption falls on the people who had finally learned how to use the previous version.
The replacement may be more capable, but capability does not make the transition costless.
Anyone who has built software or structured workflows on top of language-model APIs will recognise the same problem on a smaller scale. A silent model update can alter formatting, tool selection, refusal behaviour or the way a model handles an awkward edge case. A system that once returned valid JSON may start producing structures that break the application consuming them. A model may become better at the general task while becoming less predictable on the particular task a business relies on, a mismatch I wrote about from the user's side in The Middle.
In traditional software, we recognise the difference between an improvement and a breaking change. In AI, a release can improve benchmark performance while quietly breaking the assumptions on which a working system depends. What a working system needs is for change to arrive visibly, with a route through it.
What an AI LTS would promise
Imagine a major AI lab designating a capable model as a five-year Long Term Support release. The commitment would be more substantial than leaving an old model name in an API menu. It would establish a defined relationship between the provider and the people building on its technology.
Three commitments would form the basis of such a release.
1. Versioned behaviour and controlled change
The model checkpoint, inference configuration and interfaces would be documented and versioned. Providers would publish compatibility criteria and maintain regression tests covering the tasks and output formats on which downstream applications depend.
The aim would not be to promise that every prompt produces an identical answer forever. Language models are probabilistic, and outputs can vary even when the underlying weights remain unchanged. Behaviour can also depend on system prompts, inference software, safety filters, tool definitions and other parts of the serving stack.
The aim would be to make material changes visible, measurable and controlled. A provider should not silently alter a supported release in ways that invalidate existing workflows. Where a change is necessary, it should be documented, tested and accompanied by a migration path.
2. Security and safety maintenance without unnecessary disruption
An LTS model would still need security updates and improvements to its safeguards. Stability cannot mean preserving a vulnerability simply because fixing it might change behaviour.
The provider would distinguish routine maintenance from changes that materially affect model behaviour, publish change notes, and test updates against regression suites covering both safety and task performance.
Sometimes those objectives will conflict. A serious vulnerability may require a change that breaks an existing workflow, and an urgent security issue may not allow a long migration period. The commitment should be to explain those decisions, minimise unnecessary disruption and provide a clear route forward, not to pretend that safety and compatibility can always be reconciled perfectly.
3. Predictable availability and economics
Institutions would receive a defined support period, meaningful notice before retirement, transparent pricing or agreed pricing terms, and a documented migration path when support ends.
A model that remains technically available but becomes prohibitively expensive is not a dependable foundation, and as I argued in The Meter, consumer AI has already shown how little of this pricing is built to be planned around. Nor is a model dependable if its provider can withdraw it at short notice to free up computing capacity for a newer release.

report.summary: A UK college lecturer argues the AI industry needs Ubuntu-style long-term support releases so schools, hospitals and developers can depend on stable, maintained models instead of constant migration.
report.background: AI discourse is fixated on the frontier: every few weeks a new model tops a leaderboard with a bigger context window or better benchmark scores, and the whole ecosystem is expected to rewrite prompts and migrate. Linux solved this decades ago by splitting release cycles — Ubuntu ships an LTS every two years and maintains it for five, while interim releases serve anyone who wants novelty. A supported release is not frozen: bugs and vulnerabilities get fixed, but the release itself stays put. AI has no equivalent commitment. Pinned model snapshots and enterprise deprecation windows offer partial stability, but pinning is not a guarantee of maintenance or compatibility. The closest thing is Anthropic's November 2025 pledge to preserve the weights of publicly released models for the lifetime of the company — which protects the model, not the people who built workflows around it. Meanwhile, cautious institutions with constrained budgets absorb the disruption.
key_points: Frontier churn is the only metric the industry tracks. Each model release with a larger context window or a few benchmark points gain pushes organisations to re-evaluate tools, rewrite prompts and retrain staff. The author argues that slowing the frontier would give everyone else time to absorb, learn and institutionalise what already exists.

Preserved weights are not a support window. Anthropic's promise to keep public model weights available protects the model itself; an LTS commitment would protect the organisations whose training, safeguarding procedures and student guidance depend on a specific model's behaviour.

Migration costs are real and unevenly distributed. A college may spend six months building an accessible teaching workflow — training staff, testing edge cases, writing guidance — then lose it when a model is deprecated. The replacement may be more capable, but capability does not make the transition free.

An AI LTS would need three commitments: documented, versioned checkpoints and interfaces with published regression tests; security and safety maintenance that is clearly separated from behaviour-changing updates; and predictable support periods, notice and pricing so institutions can plan.

Silent updates break working systems. A model can improve on general benchmarks while quietly changing formatting, tool selection or refusal behaviour, breaking downstream applications that relied on the old behaviour — a breaking change nobody labelled as one.
report.impact: For AI labs, an LTS model would mean maintaining older serving stacks and regression suites alongside frontier work — an operational cost, but also a way to win regulated and public-sector customers who currently cannot commit. For developers, it would turn silent model updates into versioned, documented events with migration paths, making production systems on proprietary APIs far less fragile and reducing the appeal of self-hosting purely for stability. For regular users, the benefit is quieter: the tools they learn, and the institutional workflows built around them, stop being pulled out from under them every few months. The risk is a two-tier ecosystem where the frontier races ahead while supported models age — but that is exactly the trade-off Linux accepted decades ago.
report.tools: Watch for model-pinning and versioning features from API providers (OpenRouter, Anthropic, OpenAI snapshot names), plus self-hosting stacks like Ollama, LM Studio and vLLM for running open-weight models locally to escape deprecation risk. For regression testing and prompt versioning around a fixed model, look at LangSmith, Braintrust and PromptLayer. Hugging Face model repositories and the open-weight releases from Meta, Mistral and Qwen remain the most practical route to long-term continuity today.
